summary: Describes the services that the LSMA group found necessary for large-scale distributed simulation over multicast, and the aspects of the Internet protocols that need more development to meet those needs. It is informational and reads as a requirements and gaps document.

plainLanguage.summary: This memo looks at what the Internet's protocols cannot yet do for large distributed simulations, where many computers share one virtual world and people interact with it in real time. It lists the services such a system needs, from predictable delivery with little loss to fast joining of multicast groups, and then names the parts of the protocol suite that fall short of them.

questions: internet protocol gaps for large scale simulation
subtitle: What the Internet protocols lack for large distributed simulations, where thousands of hosts must exchange state data in real time.

tldr.problem: Large distributed simulations put thousands of hosts on shared wide-area networks, exchanging state data in real time with strict limits on latency and loss. The Internet protocol suite does not offer everything such a system needs.
tldr.mechanism: The memo lists the six services the Large-Scale Multicast Applications working group found necessary, then walks through the areas where today's protocols fall short: reservation at scale, multicast over ATM, reliable multicast, management, session control, naming, security and inter-domain multicast.
tldr.outcome: The memo is Informational and reads as a requirements and gaps document. Its purpose is to inform the IETF so that it can produce protocols meeting these needs; it defines no protocol itself.

facts.label: Simulated objects in the DoD goal

today: RFC 2502 is an Informational memo from February 1999 and has not been obsoleted or updated. It is a requirements and gaps document: it sets no standard, and the memo's stated purpose is to inform the IETF so that it can produce protocols that meet the needs it describes.

sections.title: The Large Multicast Environment
sections.content:
The Large-Scale Multicast Applications (LSMA) working group was chartered to produce documents aimed at a consensus-based development of the Internet protocols to support large scale multicast applications, including real-time distributed simulation. This memo defines the services LSMA found to be required and the aspects of the Internet protocols it found to need further development.

Distributed Interactive Simulation (DIS) is the name of a family of protocols used to exchange information about a virtual environment among hosts in a distributed system that are simulating the behaviour of objects in that environment. The objects are capable of physical interactions and can sense each other by visual and other means. DIS was developed by the U.S. Department of Defense for military training, rehearsal and other purposes. Its successor is the High Level Architecture for simulation (HLA).

The feature that drives the network requirements is that these systems are intended to work with output to and input from humans across distributed simulators in real time. That places tight limits on latency between hosts, and it means any practical network has to multicast to distribute all data to all participating simulators. Large configurations are expected to group hosts on multicast groups based on sharing the same sensor inputs, which can mean a need for thousands of multicast groups where objects move between groups in large numbers at high rates.

The total data rate is bounded, because the number of simulators is known in advance and their maximum output rate in packets per second and bits per second is specified. The required data rate in any particular group cannot be predicted, and may change quite rapidly during the simulation. The real time flow consists of packets of length around 2000 bits at rates from 0.2 packets per second per simulator to 15 packets per second per simulator. This information is intentionally redundant and is normally transmitted with a best-effort transport protocol (UDP), and in some cases it is compressed. In tightly coupled simulations such as high performance aircraft, the maximum acceptable latency is 100 milliseconds between any two hosts. At relatively rare intervals events such as collisions may occur which require reliable transmission of some data, on a unicast basis, to any other host in the system.

The U.S. Department of Defense has a goal to build distributed simulation systems with up to 100,000 simulated objects, many of them computer generated forces that run with minimal human intervention. Beyond the Department of Defense, many people see a likelihood that distributed simulation capabilities may be commercialised as entertainment, and such a system could conceivably be larger than the Department of Defense goal.

HLA is a Department of Defense development beyond DIS that brings DIS and other forms of distributed simulation into a unifying system paradigm. From a distributed systems standpoint HLA is considerably more sophisticated: attributes of distributed objects may be controlled by different simulators. From the standpoint of the supporting network the primary difference is that HLA does not call for redundant transmission of object attributes; instead it specifies a Run Time Infrastructure (RTI) that is responsible for transmitting data reliably, and may do so by various means including redundant transmission using best effort protocols. HLA has similar requirements for many-to-many transmission of object attributes at rates in excess of one update per object per second that cannot be met without multicasting, and it calls for transmission of semantically organized data in that many-to-many context.

One approach to these challenges has been to aggregate the contents of many multicast groups into a single multicast transmission, a technique termed dual-mode or bi-level multicast. It takes advantage of the fact that although the amount of traffic in any particular multicast group can vary greatly, the aggregate of all transmissions is bounded. It also bounds the network control problem of group joins, because the joins take place among dedicated collections of routers and across dedicated switched virtual circuits rather than contending with other large multicast applications sharing the same network. The cost is a new, nonstandard aggregation element that is a hybrid of the Internet and ATM protocols.
sections.plainLanguage: These simulations put thousands of computers into one shared virtual world, and people watch and act in it in real time. That means the data has to arrive quickly, and it has to reach every participant, so the network has to send the same data to a group rather than to each computer one at a time. The newest design, HLA, differs from DIS in that it does not send everything redundantly; instead a separate piece of software, the Run Time Infrastructure, is responsible for getting the data across reliably.

sections.title: The Network Services Required
sections.content:
The memo lists six services that the network must provide.

  • Real-time packet delivery, with low packet loss (less than 2%), and predictable latency on the order of a few hundred milliseconds after buffering to account for jitter (variation of latency), such that less than 2% of packets fail to arrive within the specified latency, in a shared network.
  • Multicasting with thousands of multicast groups that can support join latencies of less than one second, at rates of hundreds of joins per second.
  • Multicasting using a many-to-many paradigm in which 90% or more of the group members act as receivers and senders within any given multicast group.
  • Support for resource reservation. Because it is impractical to over-provision the WAN and the LAN for large distributed simulations, it is important to be able to reserve an overall capacity that can be dynamically allocated among the multicast groups.
  • Support for a mixture of best-effort and reliable low-latency multicast transport, where best-effort predominates in the mixture, and the participants in the reliable multicast may be distributed across any portion of the network.
  • Support for secure networking, in the form of per-packet encryption and authentication needed for classified military simulations.
sections.plainLanguage: The list is short and specific. Delivery has to be fast and lose less than 2 percent of packets. Groups have to be joinable in under a second, and hundreds of joins a second has to work. Most members of a group are both sending and receiving. Capacity has to be reservable. Most traffic can be best-effort, but some has to be reliable. And every packet has to be able to be encrypted and checked.

sections.title: Reservation, Multicast over ATM and Reliable Transport
sections.content:
Large-scale resource reservation. RSVP is aimed at providing setup and flow-based information for managing information flows at pre-committed performance levels, and this capability is generally seen as needed in real-time systems such as the HLA Run Time Infrastructure. Concerns have been raised about the scalability of RSVP and about its ability to support highly dynamic flow control changes. The requirement in LSMA is for rapid change of group membership, not for rapid change of group reservations, because in existing Run Time Infrastructures the aggregate requirement for all groups in a large scale distributed simulation is static. The current RSVP draft standard for LSMA does not support aggregation of reservation resources for groups of flows and therefore does not meet the needs of existing Run Time Infrastructures. There is also at least one Run Time Infrastructure development underway that intends to use individual, dynamic reservations for large numbers of groups, which would require a dynamic resource reservation capability that scales to thousands of multicast groups.

RSVP also provides support only for communicating specifications of the required information flows between simulators and the network, and within the network. Distributing routing information among the routers within the network is a different function altogether, performed by routing protocols such as Multicast Open Shortest Path First (MOSPF). To provide effective resource reservation in a large shared network it may be necessary to have a routing protocol that determines paths through the network within the context of a quality of service requirement, an example being the proposed Quality Of Service Path First (QOSPF) routing protocol. The memo notes that the requirement for resource-sensitive routing will be difficult to define before LSMA networks are deployed with RSVP.

IP multicast over ATM. Multicast takes advantage of the efficiency obtained when the network can recognise and replicate packets destined for a group of locations, so that the network provides duplicate copies to all destinations and greatly reduces the amount of information flowing into and through the network. When IP multicast operates over Ethernet, packets are transmitted once and received by all receivers using Ethernet-layer multicast addressing, avoiding replication of packets. With wide-area Asynchronous Transfer Mode, however, the ability to take advantage of data link layer multicast capability is not yet available beyond a single Logical IP Subnet. The memo attributes this to two causes: the switching models of IP and ATM are sufficiently different that the capability would require a rather complex solution, and there has been no clear application requirement for IP multicast over ATM multicast that provides for packet replication across multiple Logical IP Subnets. Distributed simulation is an application with such a requirement.

Hybrid best-effort and reliable multicast. The Internet protocol suite uses TCP for reliable end-to-end transport and UDP for best-effort end-to-end transport, including all multicast transport services, and the design of TCP is only capable of unicast transmission. Of the roughly 15 attempts to develop a reliable multicast transport protocol, all have shown some problem relating to positive receipt acknowledgements or negative acknowledgements, which has made real-time reliable multicast transport infeasible to date. The memo concludes that there is not likely to be a single solution for reliable multicast, but rather a number of solutions tailored to different application domains, and that approaches involving distributed logging seem to hold particular promise for the distributed simulation application.
sections.plainLanguage: Three gaps are named. Reservations cannot yet be grouped so that one reservation covers many groups, which is what a simulation with a fixed total amount of traffic needs. Multicast over ATM only works within one logical subnet. And reliable multicast has defeated every attempt so far, mostly because receivers cannot acknowledge receipt without swamping the sender.

sections.title: Management, Sessions, Naming and Inter-Domain Routing
sections.content:
Network management. Coordinated, integrated network management is one of the more difficult aspects of a large distributed simulation exercise. The technique used to support the growth of the Internet over the past several years could be expanded to fill this need. It is based on a primitive called a Management Information Base (MIB) being polled periodically at very low data rates. The receiver of the poll is an Agent, collocated with the remote process being monitored, and the agent is simple so as not to absorb many resources. The requesting process is a Manager, typically located elsewhere on a separate workstation, and it communicates to all of the agents in a given domain using SNMP. The memo finds SNMP well adapted to the purpose of distributed simulation management, in addition to managing the underlying simulation network resources, and notes that creating a standard distributed simulation MIB format would let the simulation community use the collection of powerful off-the-shelf network management tools built around SNMP.

A session protocol. Coordinating the start, stop and pause of large distributed exercises is a complex and difficult task. The Session Initiation Protocol, recently proposed by the Multiparty Multimedia Session Control working group, serves a similar purpose for managing large scale multimedia conferences. As proposed, SIP appears to offer sufficient extensibility to be used for exercise session control, if standardized by the IETF.

Low-latency multicast naming. Name-to-address mapping in the Internet is performed by the Domain Name Service, which has a distributed architecture tuned to the needs of unicast networking with reliable transmission and whose latency is not considered problematic if it is on the order of a second or more. The requirement of distributed simulation for agile movement among multicast groups implies a need for name-to-multicast-address mapping with latency of under one second for the name resolution and group join combined. This problem has been circumvented in military simulations by using group IP addresses rather than names. The memo notes that while military simulations may be satisfied with a known mapping from grid squares to multicast groups, growth of distributed simulation into commercial entertainment cannot be based on such a simple capability, because players in distributed entertainment simulations will want to be organized symbolically by virtual world and role.

Inter-domain multicast routing. Military large multicast applications typically take place within a single administrative domain, but future entertainment ones can be expected to involve heavy inter-domain multicast traffic so that players can be supported by multiple service providers. Standardized protocols able to support large numbers of multicast flows across domain boundaries will be needed for this purpose, and the memo says current work to create a Border Gateway Multicast Protocol shows promise of meeting this need.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo finds that existing tools cover most of the rest. SNMP already gives a way to watch a large exercise across many sites. SIP could start, pause and stop a whole exercise if it were standardised for the purpose. What is missing is a fast way to turn a name into a multicast group address, and a way to carry large numbers of multicast flows between different providers' networks.

sections.title: An Integrated Security Architecture
sections.content:
The memo expects the security requirement to be met by IPv6 deployment. A shortcoming of the current IPv4 implementation is the lack of integrated security. The new IPv6 protocol requires implementers to follow an integrated security architecture that provides the required integrity, authenticity and confidentiality for use of the Internet by communities with stringent security demands, such as the financial community.

The memo adds that the possibility that the IPv6 security architecture may meet military needs, when combined either with military cryptography or with government-certified commercial cryptography, merits further study.

The memo's own security section adds only a pointer: security issues are discussed in section 3.6.
sections.plainLanguage: The security requirement is expected to be met by IPv6, whose design puts the security mechanisms in the protocol rather than leaving them to be added afterwards. Whether that is enough for military use, combined with the right cryptography, is a question the memo leaves open.

viz.caption: THE SIX SERVICES THE MEMO SAYS ARE NEEDED

items.title: Real-time delivery
items.text: Under 2% packet loss and predictable latency of a few hundred milliseconds.

items.title: Thousands of groups
items.text: Join latency under one second, at hundreds of joins per second.

items.title: Many-to-many
items.text: 90% or more of a group's members both send and receive.

items.title: Resource reservation
items.text: One overall capacity, allocated among the groups dynamically.

items.title: Mixed transport
items.text: Mostly best-effort multicast, with some reliable multicast.

viz.caption: THE FIVE TRANSMISSION NEEDS IN A SIMULATION (RFC 2502)

cells: Best-effort low-latency multicast of attributes that often change continuously, such as the position of mobile objects
Low-latency reliable multicast of attributes that do not change continuously but may change at arbitrary times, such as object appearance
Low-latency reliable unicast of occasional data among arbitrary members of the multicast group
Reliable but not necessarily real-time multicast of bulk data such as terrain databases and object enumerations
Reliable unicast of control information between individual RTI components
A Run Time Infrastructure transmits reliably
